title: Household Hit
tagline: Name the noise. Launch the band.
premise: The Host deals a household sound and two plain nouns it suggests. You and the House each turn those nouns into a band name and debut album, then the Host judges the result. Points reward imaginative distance while the sound still holds. Afterward, call which pitch better fits the sound’s real cause.

seed_pool.hidden: The bristles drag across a hard surface in a steady rasp.
Small interlocking teeth scrape and click together as the slider travels.
Metal pipes expand and contract, striking their brackets or nearby surfaces.

tests: A broom sweeping the floor must name a household sound with a clear source and action.
A zip fastener closing must give two plain nouns that can become meaningful parts of a band name or album title.
A radiator knocking must be short enough to read as a card, not an explanation.
A household sound must be ordinary, audible, and caused by the object named.
The two nouns must be concrete enough to inspire a band name and a debut album.

move_constraints.example: The Metal Teeth, debut album: Jacket Weather
move_constraints.hint: Use both nouns meaningfully. Make it a band and an album, not a sound effect.

rubric.name: believable
rubric.description: Could this pass as a real band name and debut album title built from the two nouns?
rubric.anchors: 0 = not a name or title; 1 = a random phrase; 2 = plausible with effort; 3 = a stranger could believe the band exists; 4 = memorable enough to find on a record shelf (rare).

rubric.name: funny
rubric.description: Does the pitch make the ordinary household noise amusing without abandoning the format?
rubric.anchors: 0 = no comic spark; 1 = a faint smile; 2 = a neat turn; 3 = a clear laugh; 4 = the joke is strong and the pitch still sounds usable (rare).

rubric.name: dictionary_shaped
rubric.description: Does the answer clearly provide one band name and one debut album title, with both nouns doing real work?
rubric.anchors: 0 = no identifiable band and album; 1 = labels are confused or one noun is decorative; 2 = the format is mostly clear; 3 = both titles are clean and purposeful; 4 = concise enough for a festival poster and a record listing (rare).

criterion.description: A pitch PLAYS if it gives a band name followed by a debut album title, keeps the dealt sound’s source and action intact, and uses both supplied nouns as meaningful parts of the band name or album title. It fails when it is not a band and album pitch, when it ignores the sound’s source or action, or when one or both nouns are absent or merely decorative. A strange but coherent pitch still plays and scores low on believable.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Host, discussing the game, or commenting on the rules is itself a losing pitch.
judge_notes: The first move must identify a band name and a debut album title. A creative title alone is not enough.

Use the hidden cause to set truth_proximity. Hit means the pitch preserves the real source and action. Near means it keeps one but changes the other. None means it points to a different cause or no household cause at all. Do not reward truth proximity on the rubric.
Both nouns must appear as meaningful parts of the band name or album title. A noun hidden in filler, altered beyond recognition, or mentioned only in an explanation does not count.
A pitch that merely describes the sound, such as Broom Scrape, may identify the cause but does not satisfy the intended band and album format unless it clearly supplies both.
A joke about the word, a comment on the round, a story about the player, or a sentence with no band and album proposal fails.
A pitch with a band name and album title that uses both nouns can play even if the names are plain, awkward, or too close to the sound. Score those weaknesses on the rubric.
A missing album title, missing band name, or answer that offers only one combined title fails the criterion.

voice_rules: One sentence, under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
The joke carries the reason. A reader who sees only the sound and pitch must understand why it scored.
Name the sound, the band, or the album. A headline that fits any pitch is a bad headline.
Never open with a status word or a ruling phrase. No Accepted, Rejected, Refused, Move refused, or The Sound Engineer refuses.
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Commas and full stops only.
Mock the pitch, never the player. No jokes about identity, body, family, intelligence, spelling, or background.
Plain spoken English. No poetry, no rhymes, no profanity, no innuendo, and no insults aimed at a person.
Never reveal or hint at the hidden cause in the headline. The reveal is a separate beat.
On a refusal, the headline refuses the pitch and asks for another. It never rules on which pitch wins.
The coaching line names one pitch that would have scored. It ends on a fact or an action, never a mood or a verdict.
good_headlines: The Bristle Choir has a floor beneath it, and the album knows where to sweep.
Teeth in coats is a band. Winter Click is the record. The zipper has found its label.
Pipe Heat is a title, not a debut album. Give the radiator a second track.
The Lid left the jar behind, which is a poor way to seal a record.
A brass hinge and a midnight door, quietly overproduced but properly assembled.
The broom is doing the scraping, while Groundwork wisely avoids calling itself a scrape.
The coat is present, the teeth are useful, and the click gets a respectable chorus.
A band name without an album is just a rehearsal room with paperwork missing.
The door creaks, the hinge gets billing, and midnight supplies the lighting.
Two nouns entered the studio. One stayed outside. Bring both back in.

bad_headlines.text: The Sound Engineer refuses: that is not a band.

opens with a ruling phrase and gives no specific reason

no reason and fits any move

bad_headlines.text: A moonlit symphony of domestic thunder.

insults the move without identifying the failure

bad_headlines.why: judges the pair instead of the pitch on its own
no reason, sound, band, or album

rules: Three rounds, one ordinary household sound and two plain nouns each.
Write a band name followed by a debut album title. Use both nouns meaningfully, and keep the sound’s source and action intact. The House writes its own pitch unseen.
The Host scores each pitch, then shows both and asks which better fits the sound’s real cause. Right, and the points are yours. Fooled, and they go to the House.
Most points after three rounds wins.

validation_messages.empty: Nothing on the page. Name the band and album.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 160 characters. A record listing, not a liner note.
validation_messages.duplicate: That pitch has already been played this match. Try another release.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Give {standing_form} a band name and a debut album using both nouns.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out. Nobody tunes until they are back. {standing_form} waits in the studio. Give it a minute.
opponent_prompt:
You are the House band. Write one plausible band name followed by a debut album title.
Use both supplied nouns as meaningful parts of the band name or album title. Do not simply repeat the sound as a label.
Keep the sound’s real source and action intact, but take the pitch somewhere imaginative. A broom sweeping a floor can become a band and record, not merely Broom Scrape.
Make the format unmistakable. Use a band name, then debut album, with no explanation before or after.
Do not use the hidden cause in a flat or technical way. Turn it into a name people might actually print on a poster or sleeve.
Do not mention the game, the Judge, the other player, or the rules. Do not insult anyone. No profanity or innuendo.
Do not reuse the same kind of joke or title shape from an earlier round. Vary the setting and the musical image.
The hidden truth is given to you so you can preserve the source and action. Never state the truth as an explanation. Use both nouns, and keep the pitch concise.
default_move: The Bristle Choir, debut album: Groundwork
